title: เกรงใจ: the unwritten rule that explains everything
goal: Understand the values behind the way Thai people speak — reluctance to impose, saving face, keeping a cool heart — and use language that fits them.
bekal: understanding and using เกรงใจ
keeping the peace with ใจเย็นๆ and ไม่เป็นไร
complimenting, apologizing, and thanking at the right moment
behaving correctly at temples and family occasions
recognizing the words ending in ใจ that make up the whole Thai world of feelings

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — Invited to dinner at Nok's home
dialogs.intro: Budi is invited to Nok's family home. Notice that almost every sentence in this dialogue tends to someone else's feelings — and that a first refusal isn't really a refusal.

lines.speaker: แม่ของนก:
lines.text: [เชิญ|Chooen][ค่ะ|khâ] [เข้า|Khâo][มา|maa][เลย|loei][ค่ะ|khâ] [ทาน|Thaan][ข้าว|khâao][ด้วย|dûai][กัน|kan][นะ|ná][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Please, come right in. Let's eat together.
lines.literal: please — (polite). enter — come — straight — (polite). dine — rice — with — together — okay — (polite).

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][ครับ|khráp] [เกรงใจ|Kreeng-jai][จัง|jang][ครับ|khráp] [รบกวน|Róp-kuan][มาก|mâak][เลย|loei][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: Thank you. I feel bad imposing. It's so much trouble for you.

lines.speaker: แม่ของนก:
lines.text: [ไม่เป็นไร|Mâi pen rai][ค่ะ|khâ] [ทำ|Tham][ไว้|wái][เยอะ|yóe][ค่ะ|khâ] [ทาน|Thaan][เยอะๆ|yóe-yóe][นะ|ná][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Not at all. We made plenty. Eat as much as you like.

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ผม|Phǒm][เอา|ao][ของ|khǎawng][มา|maa][ฝาก|fàak][ครับ|khráp] [ขนม|Khà-nǒm][จาก|jàak][อินโดนีเซีย|In-doo-nii-sia][ครับ|khráp]

lines.speaker: แม่ของนก:
lines.text: [โอ๊ย|Óoi] [ไม่|mâi][ต้อง|tâwng][ก็ได้|kâw-dâai][ค่ะ|khâ] [เกรงใจ|Kreeng-jai][แทน|thaaen][ค่ะ|khâ] [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][มาก|mâak][นะ|ná][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Oh, you shouldn't have. Now I feel bad. Thank you so much.

lines.text: [พี่|Phîi][กิน|kin][เผ็ด|phèt][ได้|dâai][ไหม|mǎi][คะ|khá] [แม่|Mâae][ทำ|tham][แกง|kaaeng][ไว้|wái][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.text: [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][มาก|mâak][ครับ|khráp] [อาหาร|Aa-hǎan][อร่อย|à-ràwy][มาก|mâak][ครับ|khráp] [ฝีมือ|Fǐi-muue][ดี|dii][จริงๆ|jing-jing][ครับ|khráp]

lines.text: [อิ่ม|Ìm][มาก|mâak][แล้ว|láaeo][ครับ|khráp] [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][ที่|thîi][ชวน|chuan][นะ|ná][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: I'm so full. Thank you for inviting me.
lines.literal: full — very — already — (polite). thank-you — that — invite — okay — (polite).

notes: **เกรงใจ kreeng-jai is the word that best explains Thailand, and it has no exact translation.** It means reluctance to trouble others, discomfort at accepting kindness, unwillingness to be a burden. It explains why a first offer is often turned down, why people hesitate to ask for help, and why "no problem" gets said even when there clearly is one.

**Because of เกรงใจ, a first refusal is usually NOT a refusal.** ⚠️ When a host offers food and a guest says *ไม่เป็นไรค่ะ*, the offer often needs repeating once or twice. Conversely, if you're the one being offered something and you really want it, accept with *ขอบคุณครับ/ค่ะ* — no need to decline first just to be polite.

**ไม่ต้องเกรงใจนะครับ/คะ = "don't hold back, make yourself at home".** Hosts say this to release their guests, and it's a sincere permission. Once you hear it, you can take more food or mention your dietary restrictions without feeling guilty.

**ทาน thaan is the polite form of กิน kin (eat)**, and it's used for others, not for yourself. The host says *ทานเยอะๆ นะคะ* to the guest; the guest says *ผมอิ่มแล้วครับ*. The most respectful form: *รับประทาน ráp-prà-thaan*.

**เอาของมาฝาก ao khǎawng maa fàak = bring a small gift.** Arriving empty-handed isn't a big mistake, but bringing something — fruit, cake, anything small — is a much-appreciated custom. A gift from your home country is worth far more than its price.

**ฝีมือดี fǐi-muue dii = "you're a great cook", literally "good hand skill".** It's the right compliment for home cooking, and warmer than *อร่อย* alone because it praises the person, not just the food.

**เชิญ chooen = "please, go ahead".** It's used to invite someone to come in, sit, eat, or pass: *เชิญนั่งค่ะ* (please have a seat), *เชิญเลยครับ* (please, go ahead). It sounds warm and formal at once.

**Notice that Budi mentions his dietary restriction naturally, and it's received just as naturally.** Hiding a restriction to avoid causing trouble actually goes against the spirit of *เกรงใจ* — because the host would feel far worse finding out later.

grammars.title: Six values that explain how Thai people talk

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: cool-headed, patient — a highly valued trait
ให้เกียรติ
relaxed, no need to be tense

after: ⚠️ **เสียหน้า *sǐa nâa* — losing face — is what people avoid most.** That's why criticism is delivered indirectly, mistakes aren't pointed out in front of others, and disagreements are wrapped in an acknowledgment first (see unit 18). Correcting someone in front of their colleagues, even when you're right, damages a relationship far more deeply than you'd expect.

**ใจเย็นๆ *jai-yen-yen* — "calm down" — is what you'll hear** if you look annoyed. Raising your voice in Thailand almost never achieves anything except losing respect. The person who gets angry is seen as having lost, not as strong.

grammars.title: Words ending in ใจ: a whole world of feelings in one pattern
body: The word *ใจ jai* means "heart", and Thai attaches it to form almost every word for feelings. Recognize the pattern and dozens of new words become guessable.
after: ⚠️ **น้อยใจ *náwy-jai* has no exact equivalent**: a feeling of being left out or overlooked, short of anger — and usually not said directly to the person who caused it. If someone suddenly goes quiet, this is often why.

sections.title: At temples and around revered things

items: **Dress modestly** — shoulders and knees covered. This applies to men and women.
**Take off your shoes** before entering a worship hall, and don't step on the threshold.
**Sit with your legs folded back**, never pointing the soles of your feet toward a Buddha image or toward people.
**Don't touch anyone's head**, including children's. The head is considered the most honored part of the body.
⚠️ **Women must not touch a monk** or hand him anything directly. Place the item on the cloth or table provided, and the monk will pick it up.
**Don't climb on or lean against a Buddha image for a photo.** This isn't just impolite — in Thailand it can lead to serious legal trouble.
**Stand when the national anthem is played** in public spaces — at many train stations and cinemas, this happens every day at set times.

blocks.title: One topic not to discuss lightly
items: The Thai royal family is protected by very strict laws, and they apply to foreigners too, including what you write on social media.
The practical rule is simple and not up for debate: **don't discuss, comment on, or joke about the royal family** — not in public, not in casual chat, not in writing.
This isn't a matter of agreeing or disagreeing; it's a matter of law in someone else's country. If the person you're talking to brings it up, the wisest response is to smile and change the subject.

blocks.title: If you remember only one thing from this unit
items: **Your tones may slip, your manner mustn't.** A messy sentence said with a smile and a *ครับ/ค่ะ* at the end will take you much further than perfect grammar delivered in a rush or with a hard face.
Thai people rarely meet foreigners willing to learn their language, and even the smallest effort is welcomed far more warmly than you'd imagine. That holds from your very first word.
